Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
640 AM EST Wed Nov 18 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 158 AM EST Wednesday...

No significant changes were made with this forecast package.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 158 AM EST Wednesday...

1. Dry weather continues with a warming trend expected through 
the end of this week.

2. Chances for precipitation return to end the weekend, with 
colder conditions to start next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 158 AM EST Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Center of surface high pressure will remain 
nearly stationary to the southwest of our region, providing us 
with very quiet weather through this week. Temperatures will be 
about 10 degrees above seasonal normals during the day, and 
about 5 degrees above normal at night. Each day we should have 
partly to mostly sunny skies, with mainly clear nights as well. 
A low will pass well north of our region, dragging a cold front 
north of our area also. But, could see an increase in clouds 
Thursday night into Friday associated with this feature.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Our warm dry pattern will come to a halt by the 
end of the weekend as a coastal system and approaching cold 
front will drive our weather as this week ends. A robust coastal
low is expected to develop off the FL/GA coast this weekend and
up the coast towards southern New England. Concurrently, a cold
front will swing from the Great Lakes eastward towards the St. 
Lawrence Sunday. Models remain split on two narrowed solutions, 
that being a moderate rainfall event for southern/eastern 
Vermont and a more drier, light rain event favoring northern New
York and areas near the International Border. 

In Scenario 1, the coastal low hugs the east coast, phasing 
with the cold front Monday with moderate rain across southern 
and eastern Vermont. A sharp precipitation cutoff would likely 
occur with drier air limiting the northward extend of the 
precipitation. This solution, favored by the GFS ensemble suite 
shows a 30-40% chance for 0.5" areas south of US-4, and a 10-20%
chance for around an inch in Windsor County. These 
probabilities are similar for the Euro ensembles, which compared
to yesterday is an increase. That said, there are still more 
than 50% of ensemble members across the Euro and GFS that keep 
this system more offshore and point us towards scenario 2.

In Scenario 2, the coastal low tracks more out to sea with 
little to no impact to our region, with the only precipitation 
coming from the weaker cold front. Precipitation Monday would be
focused more over northern New York and areas near the 
International Border, with perhaps some isolated snow showers in
the higher terrain of the Adirondacks and NEK by Monday night 
into Tuesday. Total precipitation would be elevation dependent 
with amounts under 0.25", and many seeing under 0.1." This 
scenario is what is currently reflected in the official 
forecast. The forecast will continue to evolve as we get closer 
to the weekend, and especially since we have seen relatively 
poor model predictability with recent coastal systems this 
season already. Regardless of the precipitation uncertainty, 
temperatures will fall back towards seasonable norms to start 
next week, with highs back into the mid 30s to low 40s by 
Tuesday.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Through 12Z Thursday...Low clouds across the Adirondacks will scatter
out by 13/14Z, with prevailing VFR cigs for all terminals 
through the TAF period. A river cloud along the St. Lawrence
River is expected to scour out at MSS by 13Z, with only brief 
MVFR vsby reductions. Gusty winds aloft above LLWS height 
criteria may lead to low level turbulence in the vicinity of any
ridgetops due to mountain waves. SFC winds, outside of MSS/SLK, 
will be light 10 knots or less from the west at EFK/RUT/MPV, 
and from the south with light channeling at BTV/PBG. At MSS/SLK,
southwesterly channeled flow will increase gusts towards 20 to 
25 knots after 15Z, peaking between 17-21Z. Winds will weaken 
and subside after sunset after 23Z.
